**ARGUMENT**

**The Removing Defendant Must Show That There Is No Reasonable Basis to Predict Recovery Against the In-State Defendant.**

**A. The removing party bears a heavy burden.**

A defendant that removes on diversity grounds despite the joinder of an in-state defendant, and invokes improper joinder to escape the consequences of that joinder, must prove that the doctrine applies. Absent actual fraud in the pleading of jurisdictional facts, it must show that the plaintiff is unable to establish a cause of action against the in-state party in state court. *Smallwood v. Ill. Cent. R.R. Co.*, 385 F.3d 568, 573 (5th Cir. 2004) (en banc), *cert. denied*, 544 U.S. 992 (2005); *Travis v. Irby*, 326 F.3d 644, 646–47 (5th Cir. 2003). That burden is a heavy one. *Cuevas v. BAC Home Loans Servicing, LP*, 648 F.3d 242, 249 (5th Cir. 2011); *Mumfrey v. CVS Pharmacy, Inc.*, 719 F.3d 392, 401 (5th Cir. 2013). Plaintiff need not prove that joinder was proper; Defendant must prove that it was not.

**B. The test is whether any reasonable basis for recovery exists.**

The en banc Court has stated the test: whether the defendant has demonstrated that there is no possibility of recovery against the in-state defendant, "which stated differently means that there is no reasonable basis for the district court to predict that the plaintiff might be able to recover against an in-state defendant." *Smallwood*, 385 F.3d at 573; *see also Flagg v. Stryker Corp.*, 819 F.3d 132, 136 (5th Cir. 2016) (en banc) (applying the improper joinder standard). The possibility of recovery must be reasonable, not merely theoretical. *Smallwood*, 385 F.3d at 573 n.9; *see Great Plains Tr. Co. v. Morgan Stanley Dean Witter & Co.*, 313 F.3d 305, 312 (5th Cir. 2002). But the question remains whether Plaintiff *might* recover. Defendant cannot carry its burden merely by showing that Plaintiff may ultimately lose or that the claim will be contested. *See Travis*, 326 F.3d at 648–49.

**C. The inquiry is limited, and doubts favor remand.**

The court ordinarily conducts a Rule 12(b)(6)-type analysis, asking whether the complaint states a claim under state law against the in-state defendant. *Smallwood*, 385 F.3d at 573; *Guillory v. PPG Indus., Inc.*, 434 F.3d 303, 309 (5th Cir. 2005). The federal pleading standard governs that analysis. *Int'l Energy Ventures Mgmt., L.L.C. v. United Energy Grp., Ltd.*, 818 F.3d 193, 208 (5th Cir. 2016). A complaint that pleads a plausible state-law claim against the in-state defendant therefore ordinarily defeats improper joinder. *See Smallwood*, 385 F.3d at 573.

A district court has discretion to pierce the pleadings where the complaint states a claim but has misstated or omitted discrete facts that would determine the propriety of joinder. *Id.* at 573–74. That summary inquiry is no occasion for a mini-trial on the merits. *Id.* at 574. The court resolves contested factual issues and ambiguities in controlling state law in the plaintiff's favor. *Travis*, 326 F.3d at 649; *Gasch v. Hartford Accident & Indem. Co.*, 491 F.3d 278, 281 (5th Cir. 2007). And because removal jurisdiction is construed narrowly, doubts about its propriety are resolved in favor of remand. *Gasch*, 491 F.3d at 281–82.

The same discipline forecloses merits attacks that would dispose of the entire case. When the showing that supposedly bars recovery against the in-state defendant equally disposes of all claims against the diverse defendants, it shows only that the suit may lack merit, not that the in-state defendant was improperly joined. *Smallwood*, 385 F.3d at 574–76; *see McKee v. Kan. City S. Ry. Co.*, 358 F.3d 329, 333–35 (5th Cir. 2004).

**D. Absent the required showing, the case must be remanded.**

Defendant therefore must identify a reason, grounded in state law and a properly limited record, why the Court could not reasonably predict that Plaintiff might recover from the in-state defendant. Conclusory denials, genuinely disputed evidence, and unresolved ambiguities in state law do not suffice. Unless Defendant makes that showing, complete diversity is lacking, the Court lacks subject-matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1332, and remand is required. *See* 28 U.S.C. § 1447(c).
